note: Vectors for ledgerproof/proof-bundle/1. A conforming verifier must return PROVEN for every 'PROVEN' vector and must FAIL the named hop for every 'FAIL:*' vector. The IMPLEMENTER-TRAP entries are valid bundles that a verifier with the named bug will wrongly reject. Two vectors (malformed-hex-*) additionally pin that a hex field failing to decode is a failed check (NOT_PROVEN), never a reason to abort into MALFORMED. Two vectors (missing-required-section, required-section-not-an-object) pin the MALFORMED side of that boundary: a bundle of the wrong shape yields MALFORMED with only bundle.version run. Vectors carrying bundle_raw (a JSON string) instead of bundle exist because their defining property — duplicate keys — cannot survive a parse/re-serialize round trip; harnesses must feed the raw string to each implementation's own parser.

vectors.name: malformed-hex-op-return-payload
vectors.why: THE vector that caught a real three-way divergence, found by testing all three implementations against this exact input rather than assuming they agreed. bitcoin.op_return_payload's hex-decode was the one call in the whole verifier left unguarded (HOP 1 and HOP 3's equivalent calls were already wrapped). Before the fix: Python and Node propagated the decode exception to their outer handler and returned MALFORMED with a truncated checks[] (10 of 16 entries); Rust's `.unwrap_or_default()` already fell through to empty bytes and returned NOT_PROVEN with the full 16. Same bytes in, three different verdicts out — exactly what this suite exists to prevent. Fixed by matching Rust: malformed hex becomes empty bytes everywhere, hop4a-d fail as ordinary checks, verdict stays NOT_PROVEN with every check reported.

vectors.name: duplicate-key-last-wins
vectors.why: document.sha256 appears TWICE: first the valid hash, then a tampered one. Every stdlib JSON parser in the suite's four languages resolves duplicates last-wins (RFC 8259 leaves it undefined; last-wins is the universal stdlib behavior), so the verifier sees the TAMPERED value and hop1 must fail. Pins that the visually-first 'valid' value does not win. Carried as bundle_raw because duplicates die on any parse+re-serialize round trip.

vectors.name: duplicate-key-smuggling
vectors.why: The mirror, and the reason this class matters: first occurrence TAMPERED (what a naive grep or human skimming the raw text sees), second occurrence VALID (what every last-wins parser delivers). The verdict is legitimately PROVEN — the parsed document hash is the real one — but the raw text contains a value that never entered verification. This is the JSON-interoperability smuggling pattern known from JWT/JOSE attacks. The spec's position (SPEC-PROOF-BUNDLE §8): the bundle IS its parse; consumers who must defend against raw-text/parsed-view divergence should reject texts with duplicate keys before parsing.

vectors.name: integer-tree-size-beyond-2p53
vectors.why: tree_size = 2^53+1 (9007199254740993) in both document_tree and the log entry. The four languages PARSE this differently — Python and Rust hold it exactly, JS and Go round to 2^53 in float64 — yet all four must converge on the same verdict: hop1 fails (8 siblings cannot span a 2^53-leaf tree). Convergence holds because each implementation compares its own parsed values consistently and the verdict projection never echoes tree_size. A projection that echoed bundle numerics would diverge here — that is why it doesn't.
